dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.english: Hello uncle, how much is this jacket?

dialogue.speaker: Abu Ali
dialogue.arabic: هلا بيچ يا بنتي. هذا بخمسة وعشرين ألف.
dialogue.transliteration: hala beech ya binti. haadha b-khamsa w-3ishreen alif.
dialogue.english: Welcome, my daughter. This is twenty-five thousand.

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.arabic: خمسة وعشرين؟ غالي هواية! أكو تخفيض؟
dialogue.transliteration: khamsa w-3ishreen? ghaali hawaaya! aku takhfeed?
dialogue.english: Twenty-five? Very expensive! Is there a discount?

dialogue.speaker: Abu Ali
dialogue.arabic: القماش زين، بس عشانچ أنزّلها شوية. عشرين ألف.
dialogue.transliteration: il-gumaash zeen, bas 3ashaanich anazzilha shwayya. 3ishreen alif.
dialogue.english: The cloth is good, but for you I will bring it down a little. Twenty thousand.

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.arabic: نزّل شوية بعد. عندك أصغر منه؟
dialogue.english: Lower it a little more. Do you have a smaller one?

dialogue.speaker: Abu Ali
dialogue.arabic: أكو، هذا أصغر. أي لون تريدين؟
dialogue.transliteration: aku, haadha asghar. ay loon treedeen?
dialogue.english: Yes, this one is smaller. Which colour do you want?

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.english: Do you have another colour? I want blue.

dialogue.speaker: Abu Ali
dialogue.english: There is blue and red. Here is the blue one.

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.english: This one is nicer. What is the final price?

dialogue.speaker: Abu Ali
dialogue.english: Final price, eighteen thousand.

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.english: Okay, I want this.

dialogue.speaker: Abu Ali
dialogue.english: Go ahead, God keep you.

lessons.culture: In Baghdad's traditional markets, such as Shorja, bargaining is expected for clothes, cloth and household goods, but not in supermarkets with printed prices. Sellers call customers by family words such as عمي (uncle) or خالة (auntie), and a friendly tone lowers the price faster than a hard one.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "How much is this?"

too_formal.feedback: This is written, formal Arabic; in a Baghdad market people say it the short spoken way.

exercises.tip: بيش and شكد both mean how much; بيش is the price question at a stall.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "expensive"?

too_formal.feedback: This is a literary way to say expensive; people say غالي.

exercises.tip: غالي is expensive, رخيص is cheap.

exercises.prompt: The seller's price is too high. Ask him to lower it a little.

too_formal.item: هل يمكن أن تخفض السعر قليلاً؟
too_formal.feedback: This is written, formal Arabic; in a Baghdad market people say it the short spoken way.

exercises.tip: نزّل is the everyday bargaining verb for bringing a price down.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "_____ سعر." Meaning: Final price.

too_formal.feedback: This is written, formal Arabic; in a Baghdad market people say it the short spoken way.

exercises.tip: آخر سعر is what a seller says to close the bargaining.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Is there a discount?"

too_formal.feedback: يوجد is bookish; Iraqis say أكو for there is.

exercises.tip: أكو means there is, and ماكو means there is not.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in order: "هذا / هواية / غالي"

too_formal.feedback: جداً is formal; in Baghdad هواية means very or a lot.

exercises.tip: هواية after an adjective makes it stronger.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "blue"?

too_formal.feedback: The spelling with ق is the written form; spoken Iraqi says أزرگ with a hard g.

exercises.tip: In Iraqi Arabic ق is often said g.

exercises.prompt: The seller says: "هذا بعشرين ألف." Tell him it is very expensive.

too_formal.feedback: This is written, formal Arabic; in a Baghdad market people say it the short spoken way.

exercises.tip: Adding عمي keeps the bargaining friendly.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Do you have another colour?" (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: This is written, formal Arabic; in a Baghdad market people say it the short spoken way.

exercises.tip: ثاني means another; to a woman, use عندچ.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "بيش _____؟" Meaning: How much per kilo?

too_formal.feedback: This is written, formal Arabic; in a Baghdad market people say it the short spoken way.

exercises.tip: The seller answers with the price per kilo, for example بألفين الكيلو.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I want this."

too_formal.feedback: أرغب في is formal; spoken Iraqi uses أريد.

exercises.tip: Use هذا for a masculine thing and هاي for a feminine thing.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "This one is nicer"?

too_formal.feedback: أجمل is correct and used, but أحلى is the everyday word.

exercises.tip: أحلى is nicer or sweeter.

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.english: Sir, are you free?

dialogue.speaker: Driver
dialogue.arabic: تفضل، تحت أمرك. وين تريد تروح؟
dialogue.transliteration: tfaDDal, ta7t amrak. ween treed troo7?
dialogue.english: Please, at your service. Where do you want to go?

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.arabic: أريد أروح للمدينة القديمة. شكد الأجرة؟
dialogue.transliteration: areed aroo7 lil-madeena il-gadeema. shgad il-ujra?
dialogue.english: I want to go to the Old City. How much is the fare?

dialogue.speaker: Driver
dialogue.english: Ten thousand.

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.english: Ten? That is a lot. Lower it a little.

dialogue.speaker: Driver
dialogue.english: Okay, eight thousand. Get in.

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.english: How long does the way take?

dialogue.speaker: Driver
dialogue.arabic: نص ساعة، وإذا أكو زحمة أكثر شوية.
dialogue.transliteration: nuSS saa3a, w-idha aku zi7ma akthar shwayya.
dialogue.english: Half an hour, and a bit more if there is traffic.

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.english: Fine. Will you drop me at the station first?

dialogue.speaker: Driver
dialogue.english: As you wish, no problem.

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.english: Stop here, please.

dialogue.speaker: Driver
dialogue.english: Here you are, God keep you safe.

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.english: Thank you, God give you strength.

pair.english: Where do you want to go?

response.english: I want to go to the station.

pair.english: How long does the way take?

lessons.culture: Baghdad taxis are usually painted orange and white and mostly have no meter, so the fare is agreed before you get in, and it is normal to bargain it down. Drivers often answer a passenger with تحت أمرك or تدلل, and shared minibuses, called كيا, run set routes for a fixed price.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "How much is the fare?"

too_formal.feedback: This is written, formal Arabic; in a Baghdad market people say it the short spoken way.

exercises.tip: شكد is the everyday how much; agree the fare before you get in.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "busy" for a taxi?

too_formal.feedback: This is stiff; a driver just says مشغول.

exercises.tip: فاضي is free, مشغول is busy.

exercises.prompt: You stop a taxi. Ask the driver if he is free.

too_formal.feedback: This is written, formal Arabic; in a Baghdad market people say it the short spoken way.

exercises.tip: أستاذ is a polite way to call a driver.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "وگّف _____، لو سمحت." Meaning: Stop here, please.

too_formal.feedback: This is written, formal Arabic; in a Baghdad market people say it the short spoken way.

exercises.tip: Say it a little before the place, so the driver has time to stop.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I want to go to the Old City."

too_formal.item: أرغب في الذهاب إلى المدينة القديمة
too_formal.feedback: This is formal; spoken Iraqi says أريد أروح.

exercises.tip: أروح means to go, and القديمة is said with a g, gadeema.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in order: "الطريگ / شكد / ياخذ"

too_formal.feedback: يستغرق is written Arabic; people say ياخذ.

exercises.tip: ياخذ means takes, used for time.

exercises.prompt: What does a driver say for "At your service"?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct but bookish; a driver says تحت أمرك.

exercises.tip: أمرك alone is also common.

exercises.prompt: The driver says: "وين تريد تروح؟" Answer: the station.

too_formal.feedback: This is written, formal Arabic; in a Baghdad market people say it the short spoken way.

exercises.tip: Short answers such as للمحطة are also fine.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "What time does the bus come tomorrow?"

too_formal.item: في أي ساعة يأتي الباص غداً؟
too_formal.feedback: غداً is formal; Iraqis say باچر.

exercises.tip: شوكت means when, and باچر means tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "توصلني _____؟" Meaning: Will you drop me at the station?

too_formal.feedback: This is written, formal Arabic; in a Baghdad market people say it the short spoken way.

exercises.tip: توصلني is a polite question; for a woman driver you would say توصلين.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Take me to the station." (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: This is formal and long.

exercises.tip: خذني is the direct everyday request.

challenge.title: Bargaining and Getting There
challenge.instructions: Write and say a short Baghdadi conversation of at least 10 lines. It must include asking the price of something, bargaining it down at least once, agreeing on a price, hailing a taxi or asking about a bus, saying where you want to go, and asking about the fare or the time. Use at least 8 target phrases from this unit and include both a masculine-address form and a feminine-address form.
required_elements: A price question using بيش هذا؟ or بيش الكيلو؟
At least one attempt to lower the price, using نزّل شوية or أكو تخفيض؟
An agreement using ماشي or آخر سعر.
Hailing transport using فاضي؟ or naming تكسي or باص.
A destination using أريد أروح ل or خذني ل.
A question about fare or time using شكد الأجرة؟ or شكد ياخذ الطريگ؟
Both a masculine-address form (such as عندك) and a feminine-address form (such as عندچ or تدلليّ).
